name: Meralgia paraesthetica (LFCN entrapment)
aka: lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh neuropathy
populations: people after hip, pelvic or spinal surgery
people who wear tight belts, harnesses or equipment at the waist
summary: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment near the ASIS: burning, numbness or tingling over the anterolateral thigh without weakness. Many cases settle; evidence for injection and surgery is limited.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In the single natural-history study in a Cochrane review, 20 of 29 cases (69%) improved without treatment; most patients in a surgical series were managed conservatively

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Usually unrestricted once symptoms allow; remove the compressing factor (belt, harness, posture) and return as tolerated

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pelvic compression test: sensitivity 95% and specificity 93.3% in one surgical series of 45 patients, and 86.7% and 93.0% in a small case-control study of 30 patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Nerve conduction studies, ultrasound or MR neurography support the diagnosis; MR neurography sensitivity was at least 71% and specificity at least 94% in one study of 11 patients and 28 controls

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 50 years in a population-based series, with increasing incidence with age and BMI

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 32.6 per 100,000 patient-years in Olmsted County, Minnesota, and 247 per 100,000 in people with diabetes

overview:
Meralgia paraesthetica (MP) is an entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN), also called the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, that causes pain, paraesthesia and sensory loss in its distribution over the anterolateral thigh [r1]. The nerve is purely sensory, so there is no muscle weakness (standard anatomy). It is typically entrapped where it passes the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) (standard anatomy) [r2]. It is associated with obesity, advancing age and diabetes mellitus, and with surgery or trauma [r3,r4]. It can mimic more common diagnoses such as lumbar spine pathology, and when anterolateral thigh pain is unexplained it should be considered [r1].

The physiotherapist's role is to recognise the pattern (sensory-only symptoms in the nerve's territory, no weakness, no back signs), look for a compressive or traction trigger, use the pelvic compression test and other bedside tests with care, and reassure. The natural history is often favourable, but the evidence behind injection and surgery is limited: a Cochrane review found no randomised trials in 2012, and consensus on the best non-surgical and surgical treatments remains limited, as does research on physiotherapy [r5,r1].

epidemiology.text: In a population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota (1990–1999) of 262 patients with MP (mean age 50 years, 51% men), the age- and sex-adjusted incidence was 32.6 per 100,000 patient-years, and 247 per 100,000 in people with diabetes, about 7 times the general population. Twenty-eight per cent of MP patients had diabetes versus 17% of BMI-matched controls, the mean BMI of patients was 30.1 versus 27.3 kg/m² in controls, and most people with MP developed diabetes after the diagnosis of MP [r3]. In a surgical series of 45 patients (27 men, 18 women; mean age 47; mean symptom duration 1.9 years), 25 were managed conservatively and 20 needed surgery [r6]. In a prospective series of 26 patients who had decompression, 81% reported onset after earlier surgery or trauma [r4]. In a Cochrane review, 99 of 102 patients (97%) with iatrogenic MP recovered completely in three observational studies [r5].

intrinsic: Obesity: mean BMI 30.1 kg/m² in MP patients versus 27.3 kg/m² in age- and sex-matched controls [r3]
Diabetes mellitus: incidence 247 per 100,000 patient-years in people with diabetes, and patients with MP were about twice as likely to develop diabetes later (odds ratio 2, 95% CI 1.3–3.0) [r3]
Advancing age: incidence rose along with BMI and average age over the study period [r3]
Anatomical variation in the course of the nerve relative to the ASIS and the inguinal ligament [r2]
extrinsic: Prior surgery or trauma: 81% of one operated series reported onset after surgery or trauma [r4]; iatrogenic cases were reported in the Cochrane review [r5]
External compression at the waist or groin, such as a tight belt, waistband, harness or equipment (a commonly described trigger; not quantified in the sources read)
Pregnancy and abdominal enlargement, and positions that sustain hip extension (commonly described; not quantified in the sources read)

mechanism.summary: MP is an entrapment or traction injury of the LFCN where it leaves the pelvis, passing medial to the ASIS and under or through the inguinal ligament (standard anatomy) [r2]. Sustained external pressure at the waist (belt, waistband, harness), abdominal bulk or swelling, a tight ligament with hip extension, or surgical injury can compress or stretch the nerve; the result is a conduction block and abnormal firing in the sensory fibres, giving burning, tingling or numbness over the anterolateral thigh [r1]. The details of the mechanism are inferred from general compressive neuropathy models; the sources read did not test them in MP.
sequence: The nerve runs from the pelvis towards the thigh, passing near the ASIS and under or through the inguinal ligament [r2].
A compressive or traction load acts at this point: a tight belt or waistband, abdominal bulk, a tense inguinal ligament with hip extension, or surgical injury (mechanism inferred) [r1,r4].
The nerve is squeezed and its blood supply falls, so conduction fails and sensory fibres fire abnormally (mechanistic model).
The patient feels burning, tingling or numbness over the anterolateral thigh, often worse on standing and walking and eased by sitting (clinical convention) [r1].
There is no weakness, because the LFCN has no motor fibres (standard anatomy).
If the cause is removed, many cases improve; if the compression persists, symptoms can continue for months to years (mean symptom duration 1.9 years in one surgical series) [r5,r6].

variants.name: Idiopathic compressive MP
variants.description: The commonest form, associated with obesity, age and diabetes [r3].

variants.name: External compression
variants.description: A tight belt, waistband, harness, tool belt or protective equipment compresses the nerve near the ASIS (commonly described; not quantified in the sources read).

variants.name: Iatrogenic or post-traumatic MP
variants.description: Follows surgery or trauma near the ASIS or inguinal region; 81% of one operated series reported surgery or trauma, and iatrogenic cases recovered completely in 97% in the Cochrane review [r4,r5].

variants.name: Pregnancy-related or weight-related MP
variants.description: Abdominal enlargement may increase pressure at the inguinal ligament (commonly described; not quantified in the sources read).

variants.name: Anatomical variants
variants.description: The nerve can lie more medially than usual, which matters at surgery; in 54 operated patients the most frequent variant was type B (79%) in the Aszmann and Dellon classification [r2].

anatomy.text: The LFCN is a sensory nerve from the lumbar plexus (L2–L3) that passes obliquely across the iliacus, leaves the pelvis near the ASIS under or through the inguinal ligament, and divides into branches that supply the skin of the anterolateral thigh (standard anatomy). Its course varies; the most frequent variant in one ultrasound-assessed surgical series was type B of the Aszmann and Dellon classification, and ultrasound measured the nerve's cross-sectional area at the inguinal ligament and its distance from the ASIS [r2]. The nerve has no motor branch, so MP causes no weakness.

structures.name: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
structures.role: Purely sensory nerve of the anterolateral thigh; the entrapped structure [r1]

structures.name: Inguinal ligament
structures.role: The ligament under or through which the nerve passes; a common site of entrapment [r2]

structures.name: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
structures.role: Bony landmark; the nerve exits the pelvis close to it, and its distance from the ASIS varies [r2]

structures.name: Iliacus and sartorius
structures.role: Muscles beside the nerve's course (standard anatomy)

structures.name: Skin of the anterolateral thigh
structures.role: Territory where burning, tingling or numbness is felt [r1]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The pathological detail of MP is not well characterised in the sources read. In an entrapment neuropathy such as this, sustained pressure or traction is thought to reduce blood flow to the nerve and impair conduction, with demyelination and, if severe or prolonged, axonal injury (general model of compressive neuropathy; see the peripheral nerve injury page). The symptoms (pain, paraesthesia and sensory loss) are limited to the distribution of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh [r1]. Because the nerve is purely sensory, a motor deficit points to another diagnosis. MR neurography can show signal alteration and neuroma formation along the nerve in some patients [r7].

MP can be a mimic of lumbar spine pathology, and it also associates with diabetes mellitus beyond what age and BMI explain, which suggests that metabolic factors may make the nerve more vulnerable to compression [r1,r3].

structures.name: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
structures.effect: Compression or traction at the inguinal ligament with sensory symptoms; MR neurography can show signal alteration or neuroma formation [r7,r1]

structures.name: Inguinal ligament and ASIS region
structures.effect: Site where the nerve is most often entrapped; surgery is directed here [r2,r4]

structures.name: Skin and sensory receptors
structures.effect: Altered sensation (burning, tingling, numbness) in the anterolateral thigh [r1]

muscles.name: Thigh and hip muscles
muscles.effect: Not weak, because the LFCN has no motor fibres; weakness suggests femoral neuropathy or a root lesion (standard anatomy).

muscles.name: Hip flexors and abdominal wall
muscles.effect: Tightness or sustained hip extension may tension the inguinal ligament (clinical reasoning; not tested in the sources read).

cellular.description: Pressure reduces blood flow and impairs conduction in sensory fibres (general model of compressive neuropathy).
Persistent compression damages myelin at the site (general model of compressive neuropathy).
Many cases improve spontaneously (20 of 29 in the natural-history study in a Cochrane review); others persist, with a mean symptom duration of 1.9 years in a surgical series [r5,r6].

systems.effect: Focal entrapment neuropathy of a sensory nerve; neuropathic burning pain and sensory loss [r1].
Associated with diabetes mellitus and obesity; most patients with MP who developed diabetes did so after the MP diagnosis [r3].
Local compression from the inguinal ligament, abdominal bulk or equipment; hip posture may matter (clinical reasoning) [r2].
Persistent burning pain and sleep disturbance can affect function and mood; painDETECT, sleep and quality of life were measured in a trial [r8].

timeframes.summary: Time course varies widely. In a Cochrane review, one natural-history study described spontaneous improvement in 20 of 29 cases (69%) [r5]. In a surgical series the mean symptom duration at presentation was 1.9 years, and 25 of 45 patients were managed conservatively [r6]. No standard time frame has been validated.

healing.description: Burning, tingling or numbness develop; identify and remove the trigger (clinical convention) [r1]
Education, trigger removal and symptomatic care; many cases improve without invasive treatment [r5,r6]
Injection or further assessment when conservative measures are not enough (clinical convention) [r8,r5]
Neurolysis or neurectomy after failure of conservative therapy [r9,r10]

milestones.label: Diagnosis and trigger removal
milestones.note: Identify belt, equipment, posture and metabolic factors (clinical convention) [r3]

milestones.label: Corticosteroid and anaesthetic injection trial follow-up
milestones.note: The randomised trial followed patients to 1 month after treatment [r8]

milestones.label: Review of response to conservative care
milestones.note: A common clinical convention for deciding on injection or referral

milestones.label: Surgical reoperation-free at one year
milestones.note: 85.4% were free from reoperation at 1 year in a retrospective cohort [r10]

timeframes.returnToSport: Usually unrestricted and symptom-guided (clinical convention). Return to running, cycling or weight training as pain and paraesthesia allow, with changes to belts, harnesses and equipment that sit at the ASIS. After surgery, follow the surgeon's advice.

symptoms: Burning pain, tingling or numbness over the anterolateral thigh, in the distribution of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh [r1]
Sensation that may be worse on standing or walking and eased by sitting (clinical convention)
Hypersensitivity to light touch or clothing over the area, or a patch of reduced sensation (clinical convention) [r1]
No weakness and no back pain as the primary complaint (standard anatomy)
Possible link to a tight belt, weight gain, pregnancy, surgery or trauma [r3,r4]
signs: Reduced or altered sensation (light touch, pinprick) over the anterolateral thigh with normal strength and reflexes [r1]
Tenderness or a positive Tinel sign over the nerve near the ASIS and the inguinal ligament [r11]
Positive pelvic compression test and neurodynamic test in many patients [r6,r11]
Normal lumbar and hip examination (clinical convention)
Often a raised BMI; evidence of diabetes may be present or develop later [r3]

subjective: Distribution: confirm that symptoms follow the anterolateral thigh and stop at a clear border, not a dermatome [r1]
Quality: burning, tingling, numbness or hypersensitivity; any weakness (should be absent) [r1]
Provocation and relief: standing, walking, hip extension, tight clothing or equipment; relief on sitting or after removing the belt (clinical convention)
Triggers and risks: recent surgery or trauma, weight gain, pregnancy, tight belts, a harness or tool belt [r3,r4]
Medical history: diabetes or glucose intolerance, and previous neuropathy [r3]
Red-flag screen: back pain, bilateral symptoms, weakness, abdominal or pelvic pain, weight loss or fever (clinical convention)
observation: Posture and waist or groin pressure marks from belts and clothing (clinical convention)
Body habitus and abdominal bulk; equipment worn (clinical convention) [r3]
Gait and standing posture, including sustained hip extension (clinical convention)
palpation: Palpate medial to the ASIS and along the inguinal ligament for tenderness and reproduction of symptoms (Tinel sign) [r11]
Compare with the other side; check for an abdominal or pelvic mass or a haematoma in the region (clinical convention)
rangeOfMotion: Hip extension and lumbar extension, to see whether positions that stretch the inguinal region reproduce symptoms (clinical convention)
Hip and lumbar range to exclude joint or spinal sources [r1]
strength: Hip flexion, knee extension and ankle strength should be normal; weakness points away from MP, for example femoral neuropathy or an L2–L4 root lesion (standard anatomy)
Quadriceps strength and the knee reflex, to exclude femoral nerve involvement (clinical convention)
neuro: Map the sensory loss with light touch and pinprick: a patch on the anterolateral thigh with a sharp border and no extension to the knee or leg [r1]
Dermatome and reflex screen of L2–S1 to exclude radiculopathy, which can mimic MP [r1,r6]
Tinel sign over the nerve and neurodynamic testing [r11]
functional: Standing and walking tolerance, and whether symptoms limit sport or work
Sleep disturbance and effect on daily tasks (painDETECT, sleep and quality of life were measured in a trial) [r8]

specialTests.name: Pelvic compression test
specialTests.purpose: Help to confirm MP and separate it from lumbosacral radicular pain
specialTests.procedure: With the patient side-lying on the unaffected side, apply sustained downward pressure over the pelvis near the ASIS for about 45 seconds to slacken the inguinal ligament. The detailed procedure was not in the abstracts read; check the original papers (clinical convention).
specialTests.positive: A change in the patient's thigh symptoms with the manoeuvre. Accuracy figures come from small samples (45 patients in a surgical series; 30 electrophysiologically proven patients in a case-control study).
specialTests.sensitivity: 95% in one surgical series; 86.7% in a case-control study
specialTests.specificity: 93.3% in one surgical series; 93.0% in a case-control study

specialTests.name: Neurodynamic testing
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce LFCN symptoms with nerve loading
specialTests.procedure: Place the hip in extension and the knee in flexion, for example prone knee bend, with side flexion as tolerated, and note whether the thigh symptoms are reproduced (clinical convention; the procedure was not described in the abstract).

specialTests.name: Tinel sign over the nerve
specialTests.procedure: Tap lightly over the nerve medial to the ASIS and along the inguinal ligament.
specialTests.positive: Tingling in the anterolateral thigh. The figures are as reported in a 30-patient case-control abstract.

specialTests.name: Sensory mapping of the anterolateral thigh
specialTests.purpose: Define the territory and exclude a dermatomal or femoral pattern
specialTests.procedure: Test light touch and pinprick, comparing sides, with the patient relaxed.
specialTests.positive: Altered sensation limited to the territory of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh with normal strength. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources read.

clinicalRules.name: Sensory-only, no weakness, no back signs
clinicalRules.description: A clinical pattern, not a validated rule: MP produces pain, paraesthesia and sensory loss within the distribution of the nerve, and should be considered when anterolateral thigh pain is unexplained [r1]. Confirm with the pelvic compression test and, when needed, electrodiagnostic or imaging studies [r6,r11].

clinicalRules.name: Test accuracy comes from small studies
clinicalRules.description: The accuracy figures for the bedside tests come from a 45-patient surgical series and a 30-patient case-control study; treat them as indicative [r6,r11].

outcomeMeasures.name: Numerical pain rating scale and VAS
outcomeMeasures.use: Used as an outcome in a randomised trial and in surgical series [r8,r4]

outcomeMeasures.name: painDETECT questionnaire
outcomeMeasures.use: Neuropathic pain features, used in a randomised trial [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Semmes-Weinstein monofilament test
outcomeMeasures.use: Sensory threshold, used in a randomised trial [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) and SF-36
outcomeMeasures.use: Quality of life measures used in the same trial [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Brief Pain Inventory and Pain Disability Index
outcomeMeasures.use: Used before and after decompression in a prospective series [r4]

imaging.indication: Uncertain diagnosis, or before injection or surgery
imaging.findings: The case-control study included patients with electrophysiologically proven MP, and a randomised trial required clinical and electrophysiological findings [r11,r8]

imaging.indication: To view the nerve and its anatomical variant, and to guide injection or surgery
imaging.findings: Ultrasound before surgery was reliable for detecting anatomical variations, with 100% correlation with intraoperative findings in 54 patients [r2]

imaging.indication: Difficult cases or when surgery is considered
imaging.findings: Sensitivity at least 71% and specificity at least 94% for the diagnosis in 11 patients and 28 controls; readers showed moderate agreement for signal alteration and poor agreement for neuroma [r7]

imaging.indication: Back signs, weakness or doubt about the source
imaging.findings: To exclude lumbar spine pathology or a pelvic mass that mimics MP [r1]

differentials.name: Lumbar disc herniation with L2–L3 radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Back pain, dermatomal pattern, weakness or reflex change; the pelvic compression test helps to separate MP from lumbosacral radicular pain [r6,r1].

differentials.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differentials.distinguishing: Bilateral leg symptoms with walking, relieved by sitting and spinal flexion; may mimic MP, and the tests help to separate them [r11,r1].

differentials.name: Femoral neuropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Quadriceps weakness, reduced knee reflex and sensory loss over the anteromedial thigh and shin (standard anatomy).

differentials.name: Hip joint pathology (femoroacetabular impingement or labral tear)
differentials.distinguishing: Groin or lateral hip pain with provocation by hip flexion, adduction and rotation, without a sensory patch (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Gluteal tendinopathy or greater trochanteric pain
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the greater trochanter and pain on side-lying or single-leg stance; no sensory loss (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Inguinal-related groin pain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the inguinal canal with activity and no neuropathic territory (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Diabetic or other peripheral neuropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Stocking-glove distribution and other nerves involved; MP is itself associated with diabetes [r3].

redFlags: Weakness of hip flexion or knee extension, reduced knee reflex or sensory change beyond the anterolateral thigh: not MP; suspect femoral neuropathy or a root lesion and arrange medical review (standard anatomy).
Back pain, bilateral symptoms or bladder or bowel change: suspect a spinal cause and arrange urgent assessment (clinical convention).

Abdominal or pelvic pain, a palpable mass, bruising or anticoagulant use: suspect a retroperitoneal haematoma or mass compressing the nerve and arrange urgent medical assessment (clinical convention).
Fever, unexplained weight loss, night pain or a history of cancer with new thigh symptoms: arrange urgent medical review for infection or malignancy (clinical convention).
New diabetes symptoms or known poor glucose control: ask the doctor to review, because MP is associated with diabetes and most patients who developed diabetes did so after the MP diagnosis [r3].
Symptoms that persist or progress despite conservative measures: refer for specialist assessment for injection or surgery [r5,r6].

management.principles: Most patients can be managed conservatively, and many improve without treatment [r5,r6]. Start with an accurate diagnosis, removal of the compressive factor, education and symptomatic care. If symptoms persist, local injection and surgery are options, but the objective evidence base is weak: a Cochrane review found no randomised or quasi-randomised trials, and high-quality observational studies reported similar high improvement rates for injection and for surgery, with a comparable result in a single natural-history study with no intervention [r5]. A later randomised trial compared injection with transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) and sham TENS [r8]. Consensus on the best non-surgical and surgical treatments is limited, as is the research on physiotherapy [r1].

medical.name: Observation, reassurance and trigger removal
medical.description: In a Cochrane review, one natural-history study found spontaneous improvement in 20 of 29 cases (69%) [r5]. In a surgical series, 25 of 45 patients were managed conservatively [r6].

medical.name: Corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injection
medical.description: In the Cochrane review, four observational studies found cure or improvement in 130 of 157 cases (83%) [r5]. In a randomised trial of 62 patients (54 completed) comparing ultrasound-guided injection, TENS and sham TENS, injection gave greater improvement in painDETECT and monofilament scores than the other groups at 1 month, with no between-group difference in VAS, SF-36 or sleep scores; follow-up was short [r8].

medical.name: Surgical decompression (neurolysis)
medical.description: In the Cochrane review, 264 of 300 cases (88%) benefited from decompression in nine observational studies [r5]. In a prospective series of 26 patients, 95.8% had pain relief and 76.9% had complete pain resolution (NRS 0), with a minimum follow-up of 1 year [r4]. In a retrospective cohort of 101 patients, primary neurolysis reduced pain by a median of 6.5 NRS points and 85.4% were free from reoperation at 1 year [r10]. Uncontrolled studies with a high risk of bias [r5].

medical.name: Neurectomy (nerve division)
medical.description: In the Cochrane review, 45 of 48 cases (94%) benefited from neurectomy in three studies [r5]. A systematic review found no randomised trials and insufficient evidence to recommend neurolysis or neurectomy over the other [r9]. In a cohort, neurectomy did not give superior pain relief and is associated with unavoidable sensory loss [r10].

medical.name: Weight and metabolic management
medical.description: MP is associated with obesity and diabetes, and patients with MP were about twice as likely to develop diabetes; the authors suggested counselling on prevention of diabetes [r3]. There is no trial showing that weight loss treats MP.

medical.name: Neuropathic pain medication
medical.description: Sometimes used for persistent burning pain under a doctor's direction; no trial result was identified in the sources read (clinical convention).

physio.name: Education, reassurance and trigger modification
physio.description: Explain that the nerve is irritated at the groin, that there is no weakness or damage to the hip, and that many cases settle. Loosen or move belts, harnesses and waistbands, avoid sustained hip extension and review weight and posture (clinical convention) [r5,r1].

physio.name: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
physio.description: In the randomised trial, 10 sessions over 2 weeks of conventional TENS gave a within-group fall in VAS at 15 days, but no between-group difference in VAS compared with injection or sham TENS [r8].

physio.name: Neurodynamic mobilisation, manual therapy and exercise for associated hip and lumbar impairments
physio.description: Research on physical therapy interventions for MP is limited, and consensus on the most effective non-surgical interventions is limited [r1]. Use gentle, symptom-guided techniques and treat any coexisting hip, lumbar or abdominal-wall problem (clinical convention).

physio.name: Graded activity and general conditioning
physio.description: Keep the patient active within symptom limits, including weight management exercise where relevant (clinical convention).

physio.name: Sustained compression or stretch of the inguinal region
physio.description: Do not apply deep pressure, vigorous stretching into hip extension or tight compression garments over the ASIS (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Delaying referral when symptoms persist or progress
physio.description: Persistent or severe MP is treatable with injection or surgery, and symptoms had lasted a mean of 1.9 years in a surgical series; do not leave refractory pain unreviewed [r6,r5].

education: The nerve that supplies the skin of the outer thigh is irritated near the front of the pelvis. It does not make the leg weak and it is not a hip or back problem.
Many people improve without any invasive treatment, but it can take months.
Avoid tight belts, waistbands, harnesses and prolonged positions that press on the front of the hip bone, and review your weight and posture with us.
If the pain or numbness persists, injection and sometimes surgery are options, but the evidence for them is limited and we will discuss the pros and cons with you.
Tell your doctor about thirst, tiredness or other signs of diabetes, because MP is linked with it.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is symptom-guided and criteria-based. The core is trigger removal and education, then a graded return of hip and trunk function and activity. There is no trial of an exercise programme for MP, and research on physiotherapy for it is limited [r1]; the stages below are a clinical framework, and doses are conventions. After any injection or surgery follow the doctor's advice.

stages.name: Settle and unload
goals: Confirm the diagnosis and remove compressive triggers
precautions: Avoid tight belts, waistbands and harnesses over the ASIS
Avoid sustained hip extension positions that reproduce symptoms
Refer if weakness or red flags appear

exercises.name: Easy walking
exercises.dosage: 10–20 min, once or twice a day, comfortable pace
exercises.cues: Wear loose clothing; stop if burning builds

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic breathing and relaxed abdominal wall
exercises.cues: Soft belly; avoid bracing hard over the waistband (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Gentle knee-to-chest (supine)
exercises.dosage: 2 × 20 s, 2 times a day, if comfortable
exercises.cues: Eases hip flexion tension; stay below tingling

progressionCriteria: Symptoms stable or improving with trigger modification
Walking 20 minutes without a marked rise in burning

stages.name: Restore movement and hip control
goals: Restore normal hip and trunk range
precautions: No deep pressure over the ASIS or inguinal ligament
Keep exercise below a symptom flare

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels; avoid hyperextending the lumbar spine

exercises.name: Bird-dog
exercises.cues: Neutral spine; avoid an arched lower back

progressionCriteria: No symptom provocation with the exercises

stages.name: Strengthen and restore function
goals: Build lower limb and trunk strength
Return to normal work and leisure tasks
precautions: Avoid tight equipment at the waist during training
Stop if burning or numbness increases

exercises.name: Bodyweight squat
exercises.cues: Whole foot down; keep the trunk tall

exercises.name: Split squat
exercises.cues: Control the pelvis; avoid tipping into extension

exercises.name: Step-up
exercises.cues: Steady pelvis and knee over the foot

exercises.name: Side plank
exercises.dosage: 3 × 20–30 s each side, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Neutral hips; no pressure from tight clothing

progressionCriteria: Symptoms stable or resolving during and after training
Strength and control symmetrical and pain-free
Able to work and stand for normal periods

stages.name: Return to full activity
goals: Return to running, cycling, lifting and sport
Decide on further treatment if symptoms persist
precautions: Check belts, harnesses and equipment before sessions
Refer if symptoms persist or progress
Follow any post-injection or post-surgical instructions

exercises.name: Running or cycling progression
exercises.dosage: Gradual increase in time, 2–3 times a week
exercises.cues: Loose clothing; stop if burning returns

exercises.name: Sport- or work-specific tasks
exercises.cues: Use padding or a re-positioned belt or harness

progressionCriteria: Full return to activity without flare-ups
Patient able to manage triggers independently
If symptoms persist after about 3 months of conservative care, review options with a doctor (clinical convention)

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria exist for MP; the criteria below are clinical conventions
Symptoms (burning, tingling, numbness) absent or stable and not provoked by the sport
Compressive triggers identified and modified (belts, harnesses, equipment, posture)
Normal hip range, strength and control
Completion of graded sport-specific loading without a flare-up
After injection or surgery, clearance from the treating doctor [r8,r4]
tests: Sensory mapping and symptom provocation with the pelvic compression test
Hip and trunk strength and control tests
Sport-specific tasks with the usual equipment

prognosis: The natural history is often favourable: one natural-history study in a Cochrane review described spontaneous improvement in 20 of 29 cases (69%) [r5]. In a surgical series, 25 of 45 patients were managed conservatively and 20 needed surgery [r6]. Cure or improvement was reported in 83% of cases injected with corticosteroid and anaesthetic, 88% of cases after decompression and 94% after neurectomy in observational studies; these figures are from uncontrolled studies and the review judged the objective evidence base weak [r5]. After decompression, 85.4% were free from reoperation at 1 year in one cohort [r10], and in an earlier series the actuarial 2- and 5-year intervention-free rates were 91% and 78% [r6]. Iatrogenic MP recovered completely in 97% of cases in three studies [r5]. Because MP associates with diabetes and obesity, address the metabolic risk [r3].
prevention: Avoid prolonged compression at the waist and groin: loosen belts, waistbands and harnesses, and pad equipment (a commonly recommended measure; not tested in the sources read).
Manage weight and glucose control, because MP is associated with obesity and diabetes [r3].
Take care with positioning and surgical approaches near the ASIS and inguinal ligament, because iatrogenic MP occurs [r5,r4].
Avoid sustained hip extension postures that reproduce symptoms (clinical reasoning).
Seek review early when thigh numbness or burning appears, so that a trigger can be removed [r1].
clinicalPearls: Sensory-only, no weakness, no back signs: this triad points to MP and away from a root or femoral nerve lesion [r1].

The pelvic compression test is promising but is supported by small samples: 95% sensitivity and 93.3% specificity in a 45-patient surgical series, and 86.7% and 93.0% in a 30-patient case-control study [r6,r11].
Do not promise a cure with an injection or operation. The Cochrane review found no randomised trials, and a natural-history study reported improvement without treatment in 69% [r5].
Check the belt, harness and clothing first. Removing a compressive trigger costs nothing and may be enough.
MP associates with diabetes and obesity beyond age; most patients with MP who developed diabetes did so after the MP diagnosis, so mention glucose checks to the doctor [r3].
Neurolysis and neurectomy have not been shown to differ in pain relief, and neurectomy leaves permanent sensory loss [r9,r10].

animation.title: How the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is entrapped

captions.text: A tight belt, harness or waistband presses on the side of the pelvis all day.
Standing and walking keep the pressure on the nerve.
The nerve supplies the skin of the outer thigh, so that is where it is felt.
Burning, tingling or numbness appear over the anterolateral thigh. There is no weakness.
Obesity, diabetes, pregnancy and surgery near the groin also raise the risk.
Zooming into the front of the pelvis near the hip bone.

actions.label: Belt, swelling or abdominal bulk presses on the nerve

actions.text: Felt over the anterolateral thigh, not at the hip
Many cases settle once the pressure is removed

captions.text: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve leaves the pelvis beside the front of the hip bone.
It passes under or through the inguinal ligament, a tight spot.
Pressure from a belt, equipment, abdominal bulk or swelling squeezes the nerve here.
The sensory fibres fire abnormally and then conduct poorly.
The result is burning, tingling or numbness over the anterolateral thigh. It is a sensory nerve, so there is no weakness.
If the pressure is removed, many cases settle. Injection or surgery is for persistent cases.
A healthy nerve: myelinated fibres fed by small blood vessels.
Compression: pressure starts to block the signal. The drawing is a general model of entrapment (schematic).
Reduced blood supply to the nerve impairs conduction.
Persistent pressure damages the myelin and slows conduction.
Recovery depends on removing the pressure. This is a general nerve model, not MP-specific data.
